en: The Sutra of the Girl Vimalā, also known as the Dharma Gate of Eloquence in Discourse, translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.

At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who were free from further afflictions, whose minds had attained mastery, who were well-liberated in mind and well-liberated through wisdom, the great dragons among men, who had done what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, possessed right knowledge and a liberated mind, were freed from everything, had attained mastery over their hearts, and had reached the supreme shore—with the sole exception of the Venerable Ānanda; all the others were great arhats.
There were ten thousand great bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive and bound by only one more birth. Their names were:

Bodhisattva Jewel Radiance, Bodhisattva Accumulation of Wisdom, Bodhisattva Supreme Treasury, Bodhisattva Renowned Intent, Bodhisattva Accumulation of Eloquence, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Bodhisattva Maitreya, Bodhisattva Attainment of Freedom from Sorrow, Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, Bodhisattva Unconfused Conduct, Bodhisattva Unconfused Vision, Bodhisattva Evil-Remover, Bodhisattva Destroyer of All Darkness of Compassion, Bodhisattva Adorned with the Jewel Flower of Merit, Bodhisattva Golden Tassel Radiant Virtue, Bodhisattva Obstructor of All Sins, and Bodhisattva Indestructible Contemplation. With these as their leaders, there were ten thousand such bodhisattvas together.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Aniruddha, and the Venerable Ānanda— these [as follows]:
These eight great śrāvakas— Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta Bodhisattva,
Vimalamati Bodhisattva, Ratnaketu Bodhisattva, Avimuktidarśana Bodhisattva, Sarvapāpavaraṇaviśodhana Bodhisattva,
Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Sthiramati Bodhisattva, and Acintyagati Bodhisattva— these eight bodhisattvas...
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, together with the great Śrāvakas, at the time of dawn, donned their robes, took up their alms bowls, and clad themselves in saffron-colored garments;
they went forth together, intending to enter the city of Śrāvastī for the purpose of begging for food.
Before reaching that city, while still on the road, they said to one another:
"Let us abide in the samādhi of 'form as it is' and enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms."
"In this way, if one enters the city of Śrāvastī, all the people will be able to hear the Noble Truths.
The Venerable Śāriputra said,
"My mind abides in the *rūpa-samādhi*, and I shall enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms."
Likewise, if he enters the city of Śrāvastī, all the people will attain unimpeded wisdom regarding the Noble Truths and indestructible wisdom; that wisdom shall not be obscured.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said:
"My mind dwells securely in the Samādhi of the Nature of Form as it Is; thus I enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
In this way, when I enter the city of Śrāvastī, no member of the populace shall be subject to the works of Māra."
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa said:
"My mind dwells in the *samādhi* of the 'form-as-it-is' (*rūpa-tathatā-samādhi*), and I enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Thus, if anyone—whether women or men, whether male or female—gives me food and drink upon my entering the city of Śrāvastī, they shall all obtain inexhaustible merit and reward, leading even unto *nirvāṇa*."
The Venerable Subhūti said:
"My mind dwells in the samādhi of the 'form-as-it-is' (yathā-rūpa), and thus I enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
In this way, if one enters the city of Śrāvastī, all its inhabitants shall attain the state of an araṇya-dweller."
The Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"My mind dwells securely in the samādhi of 'form-as-it-is,' and I have entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food."
"In this way, if one enters the city of Śrāvastī, all the people will attain samādhi.
The Venerable Revata said, "My mind dwells securely in the Samādhi of Form; thus I shall enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms."
Likewise, if he enters the city of Śrāvastī, all the non-Buddhists, the Carakas, Parivrājakas, Kāṇḍins, Ājīvikas, Brahmins, and householders will not harbor evil views.
The Venerable Aniruddha said:
"My mind dwells in the *samādhi* of 'form-as-it-is,' and I enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
In this way, when I enter the city of Śrāvastī, all the people there shall attain joy free from envy."
Venerable Ānanda said: "My mind dwells in the *samādhi* of the form of space as it is; thus I enter the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
In this way, when I enter the city of Śrāvastī, all the people hear the Dharma and immediately understand it."
The youth Mañjuśrī said:

"My mind dwells in peace, contemplating all things as they truly are. Thus, when I enter the city of Śrāvastī, from the gates, windows, walls, vessels, ornaments, leaves, flowers, fruits, and even the saṃghāṭī robes, there issue forth sounds of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; sounds of non-arising and sounds of arising; and sounds of selflessness."
The Bodhisattva Remover of Evil said:

"My mind dwells in peace, observing things as they are, such as form. Thus, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, those sentient beings there who have committed evil deeds and ought to undergo retribution will, by virtue of seeing this Dharma, experience it lightly in their present lives."
The Bodhisattva Ratnaketu said:
"My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form; likewise, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, all treasuries filled with excellent jewels will open."
The Bodhisattva Non-deluded Vision said:
"My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form; likewise, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, what kind of sentient beings will be capable of attaining bodhi?"
Whether they be women, husbands, men, or women, all who see me with their eyes shall behold my body as having the color of a Buddha’s body, and they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Obstructing All Sins said:
"My mind dwells in peace, observing all things as they truly are; thus, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, no member of the populace shall be obstructed by the five hindrances."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said:

“My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form; likewise, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, whatever sentient beings are bound, held captive, or about to be executed shall all attain liberation and be free from fear.”
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said:

"My mind dwells securely in the contemplation of form as it truly is. Thus, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, all the people—whatever sentient beings may have malevolent minds—will turn toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness, praising and extolling each other, so that their voices and speech shall all attain eloquence."
The Bodhisattva Amuḍhacārin said:

"My mind dwells in peace, observing all things as they are, such as form. Thus, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, whatever sentient beings see me with their eyes shall all never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, those great śrāvakas and those bodhisattvas, relying upon such a Dharma and practicing and teaching in such a manner, proceeded together toward the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala had a daughter named Vimalāprāptā. She had already drawn near to immeasurable Buddhas in the past, long planted roots of goodness, made offerings to many Buddhas, and understood the profound Dharma. She had attained the five supernormal powers—her divine eye saw afar, pure and surpassing that of humans—and she could hear from a great distance everything said by those bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas as they conversed on the road.
She was of upright and charming appearance, peerless and exceedingly lovely.
Endowed with exquisite beauty, she was the delight of her parents; all the court ladies and all the people were joyful to behold her, and she was then twelve years of age.
On the eighth day of the second month, under the constellation Puṣya, he resolved to go out on an excursion to seek auspicious signs.
His parents granted him permission, and he was accompanied by five hundred Brahmins.
Carrying ghee, curd, flowers, grass, and ritual vessels, he went forth accompanied by them, intending to perform a ritual for that Brahmin.
Upon seeing the various Bodhisattvas and Great Śrāvakas, he immediately stopped and thought to himself:
"I now behold these auspicious signs and noble persons."
At that time, among the brahmins who were his attendants, there was an elder brahmin named Brahmā, also known as Vimalaprabha, who spoke these words:
"Young woman, you should know that this which I have seen is an inauspicious omen."
Since there are bhikṣus staying ahead as described, you may turn back and enter the city.
Seeing such omens, whatever is undertaken will not be auspicious.
For this reason, whether through interpretation or memorializing [the king], it will not be auspicious nor will it succeed.
At that very moment, the girl Vimalā addressed the Brahmin Brahmā in verse:
"Beholding this unobstructed excellence, Which can dispel the evils of many,
One sees the purity of the Four Truths, And through right mindfulness, attains faith and liberation."
To those supreme fields of merit among two-legged beings, One who gives with the wish to be born in heaven Obtains the fruit of ambrosia; The giver shall not meet with evil.
The foremost among those who uphold the precepts, Free from turbidity and devoid of evil thoughts—
He travels through the world to treat illnesses, healing and saving suffering sentient beings.
The Buddha is the most supreme in the world, the foremost Lord of Dharma;
this one is his son, untainted by any dust or defilement.
These great bodhisattvas have distanced themselves from what?
They have distanced themselves from all unwholesome dharmas, always being cautious and never transgressing.
Their upholding of the precepts is supreme in the world; those who see such good people are truly blessed.
By making an offering as small as a speck of dust, one obtains wealth in accordance with the Dharma.
This is the mark of fulfillment; this is the field of merit purified by a virtuous mind.
When a Brahmin gains faith, they obtain great blessings and are reborn among humans.
At that time, the brahmin Brahmādeva spoke these verses for the sake of the maiden Vimalā:

"Do not speak according to a deluded mind; When observing a bhikṣu during the time of the fast, Though he be one who wears the robes and has shaved his head, Do not seek auspiciousness through seeing him."
The Venerable One will not be pleased with you this morning;
I shall surely be ridiculed for failing to observe the fast and precepts. I pray that you do not look upon the bhikṣu.
If you do not look upon the bhikṣu, that would be most excellent.
At that time, the girl Vimalā spoke these verses to the brahmin Brahmā:
"It was not this very day that could save my parents;
Neither were my kinsmen, nor wealth, Nor even fine ornaments."
This person of such merit enters into conditioned existence;
this person can save me, and likewise save my parents.
This very morning, I shall relinquish both body and life.
I deeply cherish and delight in the Buddha-dharma, desiring no worldly wealth or pleasure.
There is no other refuge that can protect sentient beings;
only the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—the Triple Gem—can provide protection.
At that time, the brahmin Brahmā said to the girl Vimalā:
“You are greatly in error.
From the past until now, you have never seen a Buddha, you have never heard the Dharma, and you have never made offerings to the Saṅgha.”
“Where did you hear this? How do you place your faith in the Buddha?
The girl Vimaladattā replied as follows:

“Seven days after my birth, a brahmin placed my body upon a bed of gold and jewels within a sandalwood palace; at that time, five hundred devaputras were passing through the air above me, and I saw them.”

At that time, among those five hundred devaputras, there was one devaputra who had previously seen the Tathāgata; he offered various praises, spoke of the Buddha’s merits, and extolled the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
At that time, I heard five hundred devaputras all questioning him together, saying:
"Did you see the Buddha coming? What was the Buddha’s appearance like?"
"How can this be known?
At that time, the deva-son, perceiving the faith in my mind and desiring to inspire faith in five hundred deva-sons, spoke these verses:
"Your hair is free from the stains of desire, Pure, soft, and curling."
His face is like a hundred-petaled flower, Like the full moon in a cloudless night sky;
The color of his ūrṇā-hair is like snow or crystal, And the space between his brows is most delightful.
He is the most excellent among all his kinsmen, And the Buddha’s speech is exceedingly subtle and wondrous.
The Lord of Men has lion-like jaws, with eyes most exquisite;
his forty teeth are even and level, and he is the supreme being among all living creatures.
Furthermore, he possesses a broad and long tongue, and a face that is perfectly pure and complete.
Beneficial and virtuous speech, free from harsh words and double-tongued talk;
without idle chatter, the Buddha neither slanders nor praises,
but benefits all sentient beings, so that countless beings place their faith in him.
The nape of his neck is like a conch shell; the arms and fingers of this man are long, like the trunk of a royal elephant. Rare and pure, he enters the retreat;
his private parts are concealed like those of a royal elephant, and he is also like the radiance of the sun.
The hairs of his body all point upward; his feet are like those of a deer, with soles that are level.
Free from defilement and evil, he speaks words of truth.
All you Kings of Munis, you have already destroyed wrong views; all wrong views have been utterly extinguished.
When sentient beings pose billions of difficult questions, you answer correctly to bring them joy;
remaining far removed from those two extremes, you preach the Dharma of the Middle Way.
Whosoever hears it shall attain the supreme bliss of nirvana.
Direct and not crooked, his speech is victorious; all rejoice and love it.
The cloud of Dharma covers everywhere, raining the rain of Dharma with impartiality.
Having himself crossed over, the Tathāgata likewise delivers those sentient beings.
"Returning to save others is foremost; observing what accords with the world, my other immeasurable merits I cannot fully describe.
Having heard this, that deva’s mind was opened and he conceived pure faith in the Buddha.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the girl Vimalā addressed the brahmin Brahmā, saying: "Great Brahmin!
Seven days after my birth, I was able to hear of these merits of the Buddha-dharma."

From that time forth, there has never been even a moment when his mind was obscured by delusion; he did not cling to sensual desires, did not cling to envy, did not cling to greed, and did not give rise to a thieving mind;
his mind neither deliberated nor recollected, and he felt no attachment—whether toward father or mother, brother or sister, or any other relative.
He does not give rise to attachment toward objects of adornment;
he does not give rise to attachment toward kings, capitals, towns, villages, or even his own life. Great Brahmin!
I recall a distinct characteristic, namely, the characteristic of a Buddha.
Great Brahmin! My mind constantly and perpetually recollects these three things.
What are these three?
In whichever direction the Tathāgata may travel, I shall question the Tathāgata;

and whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, I shall fully comprehend it all—without missing a single word, without missing a single meaning, and without missing a single phrase—for not even a single night or a single day.
"Wherever I may be, I always see the Buddha; it is not that I do not see him. I always hear the Dharma and always make offerings to the Sangha, O Great Brahmin!"
"Beholding the Buddha in this way, hearing the Dharma in this way, and making offerings to the Sangha, I am never satiated.
At that time, the Great Brahmin Brahmā commanded a companion, a minor Brahmin, saying: "O Māṇava!
"Now go back quickly; as you have received from the Stainless One (Vimala) what he has said, explain this Dharma in its entirety for the sake of the Great King and the Queen.
Then the Māṇava, having received these instructions, departed and explained this Dharma in its entirety for the sake of the Great King and the Queen, exactly as he had seen and heard it.

At that time, the girl Vimalā spoke to the people about the virtues of the Buddha as they truly are, spoke to the people about the virtues of the Dharma as they truly are, and spoke to the people about the virtues of the Saṅgha as they truly are.
At that time, having heard this, those five hundred brahmins all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Then, the girl Vimalā descended from her carriage and, together with her attendants and the brahmins, proceeded forward to where the Bodhisattva and the great śrāvakas were.
Having arrived, they paid homage with reverence and respect, stood before the Venerable Śāriputra with palms joined, and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Venerable Śāriputra!..."
All women possess very little wisdom and are exceedingly full of lustful desire.
They are exclusively given to negligence; their minds are narrow and inferior, not contemplating wholesome dharmas but frequently contemplating unwholesome dharmas.
Excellent, Great Virtue!

I only pray that you will deign to look upon me with a heart of compassionate pity and preach the Dharma as is appropriate, so that throughout the long night, I may obtain great benefit, peace, and happiness.

Before these words had even finished, King Prasenajit of Kośala, having heard the speech of the young Brahmin Māṇava, arrived with great speed and urgency. He went to where the Great Śrāvakas and the Bodhisattvas were, and seeing the girl seated there, he regarded her as he did the Great Śrāvakas and the Great Bodhisattvas, saying:
"Life at home is most joyful."
For what reason, while seated here, do you speak these words:
"From this time forth, I shall not be shrouded by delusion, nor attached to worldly pleasures, nor shall I ever give rise to such thoughts"?
Then King Prasenajit of Kośala spoke this verse for his daughter’s sake:
“You are as beautiful as a goddess, Your grace is like that of one adorned with ornaments;
Why have you conceived such an evil view, To say that nothing at all is clung to?”
The kingdom is prosperous and joyful; your mother fulfills your every wish.
Daughter, what do you have in mind that you say you find no pleasure in this body?
All hold you in honor and respect; all who see you love you.
Adorned with a hundred merits, why do you not delight in pleasure?
What have you seen or heard, O maiden, that causes you such grief and fear regarding pleasure?
Tell me with a sincere heart: what is it that you desire?
At that time, the girl Vimalā spoke these verses to her father, the king:
“O King, you do not perceive the evils of the household; amidst the fragile and precarious aggregates (skandhas), you dwell within the conditioned, like a child’s play-arena.”
In the dwelling place of venomous snakes, life does not remain for even a moment;
with no heart of peace or joy, how can one find sleep?
The four great elements are like venomous snakes; where in the three realms is there any pleasure?
With many enemies, hatred, and strife, having reached a desolate and perilous place,
surrounded by the enemies of the afflictions— how can one find peace and happiness?
What is there to enjoy in such play?
How can one be attached to pleasure?
How can one sleep after drinking poison?
How can one rejoice at being ordered to kill?
How can one find safety on a precipitous cliff?
Human life is just like this.
The Tathāgata spoke this parable: there is a mass as vast as Mount Sumeru.
With such inverted minds, who would believe in impermanent kalpas?
Parents, brothers, and the like— all are the domain of thieves—
though surrounded by spiritual friends, sons, and close kin.
Just like an image in a mirror, all things are impermanent.
What kind of person can believe in this unreality?
Upon first seeing natural wisdom, they immediately give rise to the bodhicitta.
Since first generating the mind of enlightenment, I have not lost the bodhisattva practice;
where could there be such bodhisattva practice as to be greedily attached to worldly pleasures?
I behold that Tathāgata and his inconceivable merits.
"Having heard the Dharma taught by the Sugata and having seen these sons of the Buddha, I no longer dwell upon them;
I am attached only to the pleasures of the five worldly desires.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the Kosalas, having heard what the woman said, remained silent and spoke no word.
At that time, the girl Vimalā, knowing that her father was silent,
spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra: “Venerable Śāriputra!
I wish to pose some difficult questions; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion.
The Buddha has declared that you, Great Virtue, are the foremost among those possessed of wisdom.
Great Virtue!
What is wisdom? Is that wisdom permanent or impermanent?
If it were permanent, it would contradict what the Buddha has taught: that all phenomena are entirely impermanent.
If the Buddha speaks thus, he speaks falsely and teaches a delusive doctrine.
If things were impermanent, those phenomena would not arise;
if phenomena do not arise, then those phenomena do not exist.
For what purpose is this taught?
It is to teach the Dharma of wisdom through non-recollection. For what reason?
“The Buddha has declared you, Venerable One, to be the foremost among those of great wisdom.
The Venerable Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Why do you remain silent and not answer the woman's challenge?
Venerable Śāriputra replied, "The woman did not ask me about the dharma of impermanence; she asked about the dharma of non-arising. Therefore, I did not answer."
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
The Buddha has declared you to be the foremost among those who possess supernormal powers."
Does the Venerable One manifest supernormal powers while abiding in the perception of sentient beings, or does he manifest supernormal powers while abiding in the perception of phenomena?
If he manifests supernormal powers while abiding in the perception of sentient beings, since sentient beings do not exist, how can the Venerable One manifest supernormal powers?
If one manifests supernatural powers while dwelling in the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), yet phenomena are without discrimination, so too is the Venerable One without discrimination.
Since there is no discrimination, how does the Venerable One manifest supernatural powers?
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"For what reason do you remain silent and not answer the woman’s challenge?"
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana said:

“Daughter, you did not ask me for a conceptual distinction; you asked me about non-conceptualization. Since one neither grasps nor conceptualizes the path to the Tathāgata’s awakening, I have not answered.”
At that time, the girl Vimalā asked the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "Venerable Pūrṇa!
The Buddha has declared you, Venerable One, to be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma."
"Venerable sir, do you preach the Dharma for those who uphold it, or do you preach the Dharma for those who do not uphold it?
If you preach the Dharma for those who uphold it, then you are no different from all ignorant, ordinary worldlings."
For what reason?
Because all foolish ordinary persons accept and uphold it,
O Venerable One!
In this way, you do not depart from any of the dharmas of foolish ordinary beings.
If you do not uphold or preach the Dharma, and since the Dharma is ultimately without substance, how can you, O Venerable One, be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma?
The Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra remained silent and did not answer.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa asked the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
"Why do you remain silent and not answer the woman’s challenge?"
The Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"The girl did not ask me about the meaning of conventional truth; she asked me about ultimate truth, and therefore I did not answer."
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa! Venerable One, you enter the eight liberations, and having entered them, you emerge from them to preach the Dharma for others."
If even those who receive as little as a single ladle of food from such a person are all reborn in heaven,
how then do they give to one of great virtue?
Is it a pure gift of the body?
Is it a pure gift of the mind?
Or is it a pure gift of both body and mind?

If one gives the body as a pure gift, the body is then without cognition, without sensation, and immobile—like grass, like wood, like a wall, or like earth; since the body is thus incapable of such [volition], it cannot give a pure gift.
If the mind is pure when giving, the mind is like an illusion and does not abide for even a moment; thus, one cannot give with a pure mind.
If both body and mind, internally and externally, are pure, such a body and mind cannot attain the purity of giving.
"Since body and mind are without substance, how can there be a pure gift?
Venerable Mahākāśyapa remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, Venerable Subhūti asked Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Why do you remain silent and not answer the girl's challenge?
Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied, "The girl did not ask me about taking up dharmas; she asked me about not taking up dharmas. For this reason, I did not answer."
“The girl asked me about the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), and for that reason I did not answer.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: “Venerable Subhūti!
The Buddha has said that the practice of the great virtuous one in the araṇya is the foremost.
Venerable One! As for this araṇya, is it something that is cultivated?
Is it for the sake of a dharma that one practices? If there were a thing to be practiced, it would be impermanent.

If it is for the sake of a dharma that one practices, then that dharma has no characteristic of arising and no characteristic of ceasing. If a dharma has neither the characteristic of arising nor the characteristic of ceasing, it is then equal—yet if it is equal, it is not equal; if it is suchness, it is not suchness—it is immovable and unchanging.
If it is not subject to movement or change, it cannot be described.
If it cannot be described, it is inconceivable.
If it is inconceivable, it is ineffable.
If it cannot be spoken of, then it is a non-entity.
If it is a non-entity, then it lacks reality.
If it lacks reality, the Noble One does not speak of it.
The Venerable Subhūti remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Venerable Revata asked the Venerable Subhūti:
“For what reason do you remain silent and not answer the woman’s challenge?”
The Venerable Subhūti said:
“There is not even the slightest dharma that can be spoken; silence is bliss.
When you ask about such non-proliferated dharmas, all verbal expressions are unwholesome; the realm of non-expression is the practice of the araṇya.”
At that time, the girl Vimalā asked the venerable Revata: "Venerable Revata!
The Buddha has declared you to be the foremost among those who practice dhyāna."
"Venerable sir!
Does the mind rely upon dhyāna,
or does the mind not rely upon dhyāna?"

If the mind relies upon dhyāna, the mind is like an illusion and its conceptualization is unreal; if it is thus unreal, then conceptualization is unreal, and reliance upon the samādhi of dhyāna is likewise unreal.
If there were no meditative concentration through mental application, even all the dead would attain joy;
all grasses, trees, walls, and *palāśa* trees would likewise enter samādhi. Why is this?
"Because those various objects are all devoid of mind.
Venerable Revata remained silent and did not answer.
Then, Venerable Aniruddha asked Venerable Revata:
"Why do you remain silent and not answer the woman's challenge?
Venerable Revata replied, "The Woman Vimalā has questioned the Buddha’s domain; that is not something a śrāvaka is able to answer."
Vimalā said: "What do you think?
Is there any distinction between the dharma-realm of the Tathāgata and the dharma-realm of the śrāvakas?"
If it were different from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), it would destroy the dharma-realm; if the dharma-realm were destroyed, the dharma-realm would become dualistic.
Since the dharma-realm is non-dual, it can be called True Suchness (tathatā).
Such true thusness may be called non-dual.
Such true thusness, being thus non-dual, cannot be said to be superior.
Why, Venerable Sir, do you speak in this way?
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Venerable Aniruddha, saying: "Venerable Aniruddha!
The Buddha has declared that among those who possess the divine eye, you are the foremost."
"Venerable Sir!
Does the divine eye see by means of a material object,
or does it see without a material object?"
"If one perceives that things exist, one falls into the view of eternalism;
if one perceives that things do not exist, one falls into the view of nihilism.
The Venerable Aniruddha remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Venerable Aniruddha:
"For what reason do you remain silent and not answer the woman's challenge?
The Venerable Aniruddha replied:
“Because this woman asked with wisdom, I did not answer.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
“Venerable Ānanda! [Why did you not answer her?]"
The Buddha has declared that you, Venerable One, are foremost among those of great learning.
Venerable One,
what constitutes being "of great learning"?
Is it knowledge of an object, or is it ultimate knowledge?
If it is knowledge of an object, then since the object is devoid of language, it cannot be expressed in words; it is not known by the auditory consciousness, nor is it visible.
"If one knows it thoroughly, yet the Blessed One has said: 'One should listen to the meaning, not to the words'; thus one does not listen.
Venerable Ānanda! What constitutes being 'learned'?"
The Venerable Ānanda remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason do you remain silent and not answer the girl's challenge?"
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"All letters are by nature detached, like echoes. Since you, lady, asked me about letters, I did not answer.
You asked about equanimity, which is mindless and detached from the mind; this meaning is not within the realm of those still in training—how could it be explained?"
“O Benevolent One!
You should question the Tathāgata, the Dharma King.
Then, the girl Vimalā addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Mañjuśrī! The Buddha has declared that you, Venerable One, are well-versed in the profound liberation of the Tathāgata; thus, among all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, you are the foremost.”
In what way is this dependent origination profound?
Is it profound because its nature is profound, or is it profound in itself?
If those causal conditions are profound because they are extremely deep, then those causal conditions involve no human conjunction. Why is this?
Such causal conditions neither depart nor arrive; they are not seen by visual consciousness, nor are they known by any consciousness up to and including mental consciousness.
"It arises from the causal conditions of non-dual conjunction.
If its own essence is profound, then that profound essence cannot be demonstrated. Mañjuśrī said:
"The meaning of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is exceedingly profound, exceedingly profound! Vimalaprāpta said: "Mañjuśrī!..."
"Because that ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi) is not [itself] an ultimate reality, such wisdom is therefore not wisdom.
Mañjuśrī said: "There is no one who can attain the ultimate reality through speech."
Vimalā said: “Mañjuśrī! If there is nothing to be attained, then there is no speech; because it transcends speech, there is nothing to be attained.”
Mañjuśrī said: "If that is so, how do you speak to others? Vimalaprāptā replied:
“Mañjuśrī! The awakening of the Tathāgata transcends language; it cannot be expressed.
Mañjuśrī remained silent and did not speak.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the bodhisattva Amūḍhadarśana, saying:
"Noble son, as you have said, O Amūḍhadarśana: [that all things are like illusions...]"
"My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form.
Thus, when I enter the city of Śrāvastī, which sentient beings are capable of attaining bodhi?
Whether they be women or men, whether male or female, all who see me with their eyes shall see my body as having the color of a Buddha’s body."
"What is this matter? Venerable one,
do you show the Tathāgata’s form-body (rūpakāya),
or do you show his dharma-body (dharmakāya)?"
If one were to manifest a physical body, those sentient beings would not see the Buddha's body;
yet if they were to see the Buddha's body, it would contradict the Buddha's words.
The Buddha spoke this verse:
“If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me by means of sound,
That person follows a deviant path And cannot see me.”
"If one were to point out the Dharma-body, the Buddha's Dharma-body cannot be pointed out or manifested.
Why is this? The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body transcends visual consciousness; it cannot be seen by it."
The Bodhisattva Amuḍhadarśin remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu asked the Bodhisattva Amuḍhadarśin:
"For what reason do you remain silent and not answer the woman's challenge?"
The Bodhisattva Amuḍhadarśin said,
"Because the girl asked me about that which has no substance,
I did not answer. Vimalāprāptā said:
“I do not ask about nothingness, nor is it that I do not obtain [an answer] regarding nothingness; I say that one who studies the Dharma should know it in this way.
Bodhisattva Amithyādṛṣṭi remained silent and said nothing.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu, saying:
"Noble son, you have spoken thus: [that all phenomena are empty and without self-nature]."
"My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form.
Likewise, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, all the treasuries filled with excellent jewels shall open.
What does this mean?
Virtuous one, what do you reflect upon?
Do you have a mind that aspires for merit,
or do you have no mind that aspires for merit?
If one were to have a mind that hopes for merit, O virtuous one, you would be no different from foolish ordinary beings.
Why is this? Because foolish ordinary beings all possess a mind of hope, craving, and attachment.
"If one were to have no mind that aspires for merit, then one would have no mind that aspires for accumulation.
The Bodhisattva Ratnaketu remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the girl Vimalā asked the Bodhisattva Duṣprasaha:
“Good son! You have spoken thus:
‘My mind dwells in peace, observing [all things] as being like form.’”

Thus, if he enters the city of Śrāvastī, any sentient beings therein who have committed evil deeds and ought to undergo retribution will, by virtue of seeing the Dharma, experience that retribution lightly in their present life.
"What is the meaning of this?
As the Buddha has taught, karma is inconceivable; you, sir, cannot contradict what the Buddha has said.
If you cannot conceive of karma, how can you know that heavy karma in the future will be experienced lightly in the present life?"
All phenomena are empty and without a master; how can you now say that you have attained the status of a Dharma King?
If you were able to cause heavy karma to become light, then you would be contradicting the words of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Remover of Evil said,
"By the power of my vows, I am able to cause such karma that would result in heavy retribution to become karma resulting in light retribution. Vimalāprāpta replied:
"No one possesses the power of aspiration to turn [the wheel of Dharma] back; for if there were such a turning, every single Tathāgata would have originally made this vow:
'I shall cause all sentient beings to attain Great Nirvāṇa.'"
"This gateway is not accomplished through the power of aspiration; you should know that such power of aspiration cannot turn it back.
The Bodhisattva Divyaketu remained silent and said nothing.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the bodhisattva Sarvāvaraṇavikiraṇa,
saying: "Noble son, you have spoken thus:..."
"My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form.
Likewise, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, no member of the populace shall be obstructed by the five hindrances. How is this so?
If you, O Benevolent One, practice meditative concentration, you can cause the various hindrances of sentient beings to cease their obstruction.
All phenomena are empty and without a master; thus, "you" are not "you," and "I" am not "I. How, then, could one bestow a favor upon another?
The Bodhisattva Obstructing All Sins said,
"First cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.
The Bodhisattva Attaining Freedom from Defilement said:
"All the Buddhas practice the conduct of great compassion; yet in some Buddha-fields, there are sentient beings afflicted by the fetters of the hindrances.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, remaining silent thereafter.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the noble Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"O son of good family!
You have spoken thus:..."
"My mind dwells in peace as it contemplates form.

Thus, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, whatever sentient beings are bound, held captive, or about to be executed shall immediately attain liberation; they shall be free from fear and obtain fearlessness."
"What is this matter? Do you cultivate it by grasping at it,
or do you cultivate it without grasping?"
If one grasps at cultivation, it is the grasping of a deluded person, and thus it is not permissible.
If one does not grasp at cultivation, then it is not impermanent; if it is not impermanent, then it cannot be grasped.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaṇakamudrā asked the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
"For what reason do you remain silent and not answer the woman's challenge?"
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said:

"The girl did not ask me about the dharma of arising, nor did she ask me about the dharma of cessation; she asked me about the dharma that is neither arising nor ceasing. For this reason, I did not answer."
Vimalaprabhā said: “Avalokiteśvara!
Why do you not ask where it is that there is neither birth nor cessation?”
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara said:
“Daughter Without Stain, where is there no arising and no ceasing?
There is not even the slightest movement of syllables.”

Vimalā said: "If one does not engage in the turning of [words], then all phenomena (dharmas) do not possess even a single syllable; they are not spoken by wise people through the turning of syllables. Being unattached to names and designations, the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is without obstruction; therefore, that mind is unattached."
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara remained silent and did not speak.
At that time, the girl Vimalā asked the Bodhisattva Vāgguṇarāja: “Noble son!
The Benevolent One spoke thus:
"My mind dwells in peace, observing [all] as being like form.

Thus, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, whatever sentient beings possess evil minds will turn toward one another with hearts of loving-kindness; they will mutually praise and chant, and their voices and speech shall all attain eloquence."
"What is this matter? Noble one,
does this eloquence of yours arise with causes and conditions,
or does it arise without causes and conditions?"
If there is arising by way of causes and conditions, then all that is impermanent arises from causes and conditions; if this were the case, one could not attain tranquility.
If there is no arising by way of causes and conditions, then such [arising] would lack reality, and thus it could not be said that eloquence arises.
The Bodhisattva Pratibhānasaṃbhava said:
"Since I first resolved upon awakening, I have constantly made this vow:
'If any sentient beings should behold me, may they all attain eloquence.'"
Vimalā said: "Good son! Do you possess intentional eloquence?"
Is this eloquence without mind?
If it were eloquence with mind, you would fall into the error of eternalism.
If it were eloquence without mind, then regarding those various words, how could you, O Venerable One, say that your speech is not truthful?
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa remained silent and said nothing.
At that time, the girl Vimalā asked the Bodhisattva Avimuktagati: “Noble son!
The Benevolent One spoke thus:
"My mind dwells securely in contemplation of form as it truly is.
In this way, if I enter the city of Śrāvastī, whatever sentient beings see me with their eyes shall all never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"What is this matter? What is bodhi? Does that bodhi exist?"
"Or is it non-existent?
If you say it exists, then you, O Benevolent One, are attached to permanence.
The Bodhisattva Unconfused Practice said:
"To speak of 'enlightenment' (bodhi), the wise use words to designate it as 'enlightenment.
Vimalā said: "What is that wisdom?"
Is it the nature of arising?
Or is it the nature of quiescence?
If it were the nature of arising, then all that arises is impermanent.
If all things were impermanent, then there would be no right mindfulness.
If being impermanent were itself right mindfulness, then all foolish people should possess right mindfulness.
If it is the essence of tranquility, then nothing can be apprehended therein.
If there is nothing to be apprehended, one does not discriminate,
whether it be something spoken by a Buddha, spoken by a Bodhisattva, spoken by an Arhat, or spoken by an ordinary person.

Why is this? The path to enlightenment is free from conceptual discrimination, whereas foolish ordinary beings possess conceptual discrimination; those who possess conceptual discrimination do not have wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Amuḍhacārin remained silent and said nothing.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti and the other great śrāvakas, as well as those bodhisattvas, spoke thus:
"We shall now turn back; there is no need for us to enter the city of Śrāvastī to go on our almsround."
Why is this? This morning she already obtained the exquisite food of the Dharma and was immediately satisfied.
Having heard the sublime and wondrous Dharma from that stainless woman, I too have obtained sufficient food of the Dharma this morning.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Venerable Subhūti, saying: "Venerable Subhūti!
Neither grasping nor abandoning—this is the Dharma of the śrāvakas."
"Virtuous ones, what do you now seek?
What do you keep in mind? Venerable Subhūti!"
To be free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is the teaching of the Śrāvakas; to be attached to conceptual proliferation is not the teaching of the Śrāvakas. Venerable Subhūti!
To be without reliance is the teaching of the Śrāvakas; the realm of the Noble Ones is not a basis for reliance. Not relying on or being attached to anything, one does not give rise to agitation.

At that time, those great śrāvakas, those bodhisattvas, and those five hundred brahmins, along with the girl Vimalā, King Prasenajit of Kośala, and his retinue of immeasurable people, all proceeded together to Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, she prostrated herself with her head at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and sat to one side.

The girl Vimalā circumambulated the Buddha a thousand times; having completed the thousand circumambulations, she knelt with her right knee on the ground, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and questioned the Tathāgata in verses of exquisite sound:
"I now question the Sugata, The unsurpassed and unequaled Wisdom."
The one of immeasurable, stainless name, the honored lord of the three realms,
can, through the nectar-like Dharma, cause others to obtain it through his compassionate love.
What is the practice of a Bodhisattva that enables him to sit beneath the King of Trees?
How did you destroy the army of Māra and attain unsurpassed Bodhi?
How did you cause the great earth to tremble, even shaking the palaces of the nāgas?
How did you emit radiance that universally illumines immeasurable realms?
How does one speak of the practice of the Dharma of Bodhi?
How does one attain dhāraṇī?
What is the bodhisattva practice by which one can obtain the wealth of the Buddha?
How does one cultivate tranquility, the foremost samādhi?
How does one attain the power of supernormal faculties? What does the Great Man teach?
Among all beings, what is the supreme practice, and what kind of mental conduct does he attain?
How does one attain pure eloquence, And speech that is harmonious, pure, and beautiful?
How do the various bodhisattvas Obtain virtuous retinues?
How does a Great Being Attain the knowledge of past lives?
Having attained the stainless divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds,
and the radiance of great supernormal powers, you travel through immeasurable worlds.
How do you maintain mindfulness of giving and renunciation, keep the precepts pure, and constantly practice patience?
What is diligence in dhyāna?
How does one practice prajñā?
How does one always remain far removed from the womb, the place of birth and dwelling?
No longer receiving birth from a womb, having crossed to the further shore of apparitional birth—
how is it that you abide before the Buddha and speak with your own mouth of non-self and emptiness?
How is it that regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant, those two states of mind are equal?
Having extinguished all defilements and evils, with a mind firm and free from highs and lows,
one is unmoved by worldly dharmas, just like Mount Sumeru— regardless of gain or loss,
defamation or praise, censure or eulogy, suffering or pleasure.
How do these phenomena of the world surpass the moon?
Having no master and being free from flattery and deception, and being unstained, how could there be pride?
Having abandoned the mind of self-exaltation, one possesses no such thoughts.
Tranquil and supremely serene, never abandoning *śamatha*,
how could one who possesses the foremost wisdom be bound?
Having no attachment to wife, children, or wealth, how could such things exist for them?
The craving for meditative concentration is like a bird; it is always like the moon, without difference.
Since the mind is thus, how could there be craving for dharmas?
How could there be a wise person who is like earth, water, fire, or wind?
How is it that the Immovable is eternal?
His love is as impartial as space.
How is it that he does not abandon the Dharma?
Never abandoning the Buddha-dharma, one would rather sacrifice one’s own body and life than forsake the supreme Dharma.
How does one abide in bodhi and realize the stainless Dharma?
Sentient beings conceive the notion of a physician; the Buddha-land is adorned.
How does one dwell among the pure Saṅgha?
What constitutes the pure Saṅgha?
What are the dharmas of the three periods of time?
Having heard that there are sentient beings who delight [in existence], how is craving extinguished and destroyed?
Having seen the four truths as an arhat, how is the precept-observance fulfilled?
How can one cause a hundred sentient beings to dwell securely in bodhi?
Who is able to attain physical perfection when conditioned existence involves constant attachment?
And who is there who is born through transformation?
What is great wealth and happiness? What is great wisdom?
Who is able to fully possess the practice of the path of omniscience?
How could the thirty-two marks and eighty minor excellencies be attained?
Without all such wholesome merit and virtue, how could this eloquence arise?
How could there be a pure Saṃgha, with bhikṣus receiving full ordination?
Where does this vow exist?
How do the hundred births arise?
How does past life exist?
Constantly in harmony with the Buddha throughout billions of kalpas, one performs no evil deeds but practices goodness.
With a mind unattached even to physical beauty, how could there be need for a physician?
Regarding power, diligence, and patience—how can there be superiority?
How does one take refuge in the Buddha, and how does one take refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha?
One may sacrifice even one's own body and life, yet this is not the same as abandoning the Buddha and the Dharma.
How do all sentient beings purify their conduct and practice the path to enlightenment?
By relinquishing all regrets, they preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
It is not a matter of slight delusion; they possess the great tranquility of omniscience.
"If sentient beings practice the Dharma, they shall successively receive their predictions [of enlightenment].
After the girl Vimalā had spoken thus, the World-Honored One addressed her, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
“Vimalā! You are most excellent.
You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata on such a meaning as this; listen attentively now and reflect upon it well!”
"I shall speak for you. Vimalaprabhā said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha then said to her: "O Girl Vimalā!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas are able to destroy the Māra-king. What are these four?
First, they make offerings to others without harboring envy in their hearts.
Second, abandoning harsh speech;
third, constantly generating roots of goodness in many people;
fourth, practicing loving-kindness without exhaustion.
“Vimalā! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will be able to destroy the Māra King.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Do not harbor envy in your mind, Do not speak evil words with your mouth,
Teach many people to practice virtue, And do not fail to cultivate a heart of loving-kindness.
If a Bodhisattva can practice These four kinds of dharmas,"
Having defeated the Māras of the ten directions, they realize unsurpassed bodhi. "Stainless Girl!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished four dharmas are able to shake immeasurable Buddha-worlds."
What are the four? First, acting according to what one says.
Second, having faith in the profound Dharma.
Third, firm and steadfast teaching;
fourth, the ability to teach many people toward bodhi.
Daughter Without Stain!
"If Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they are able to shake immeasurable Buddha-worlds.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Able to act according to what has been taught, Knowing the patience regarding the profound Dharma,"
Desiring to attain pure and white dharmas, and to firmly transform others,
one should always preach for the sake of many people the path to unsurpassed bodhi.
A wise person who practices such a dharma can shake billions of worlds.
“Daranirmala! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish four dharmas, they are able to emit radiance that universally illumines immeasurable buddha-worlds.”
What are the four?
First, offering lamps to the Buddha;
second, protecting and upholding the true Dharma.
Third, she is able to enter among sentient beings in the eight difficult conditions and preach the Dharma to them.
Fourth, she covers the stūpas of the Tathāgata with jeweled nets.
Daughter Without Stain!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can accomplish these four dharmas are able to emit light that universally illuminates immeasurable Buddha-worlds.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“By offering lamps to the Buddhas, One obtains pure radiance.”
They are able to protect the True Dharma and uphold it according to the True Dharma;
for those who are heedless, they preach the Dharma of heedfulness.
With nets of exquisite jewels, they cover the stupas of the Tathāgata.
In this way, these bodhisattvas emit light that illuminates the world,
pervading inconceivable billions of worlds.
When this light touches sentient beings, all who encounter it obtain happiness.
"Generating the aspiration to seek Bodhi, the unsurpassed, supreme great wisdom.
Daughter Without Stain!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain dhāraṇī."
What are the four? First, various kinds of giving.
Second, adorning women and presenting them to those who come seeking them.
Third, praising the merits of the Tathāgata;
fourth, practicing prajñā extensively.
Daughter Without Stain!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can accomplish these four dharmas will obtain dhāraṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“By practicing various kinds of giving, One then obtains dhāraṇī.”
Adorned with various ornaments, she gives them to those who come seeking;
constantly praising the Buddha’s virtues and practicing the Buddha’s Prajñā—
by performing these four dharmas, she attains the dhāraṇī.
"Able, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, to hear and retain without loss;
the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions, she can grasp through the power of mindfulness.
Daughter Without Stain!..."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas will attain samādhi.
What are these four? First, they constantly teach that conditioned phenomena are characterized by much suffering.
Second, delighting in solitude without companions;
third, exerting diligent effort;
fourth, bringing wholesome karma to completion.
“Vimalā! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"It is said that conditioned things are mostly suffering; one should delight in solitary wandering like a rhinoceros.
Diligent and ever possessing wisdom, one brings wholesome karma to ultimate completion.
By practicing these four dharmas, one seeks the practice of Bodhi."
"Having attained the samādhi of tranquility, one swiftly awakens to the Bodhi of the Buddhas. 'O Vimalā!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain the power of supernatural faculties.'"
What are the four?
First, lightness of body;
second, lightness of mind.
Third, to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas.
Fourth, to receive and uphold the equality of the four elements and the space element.
O daughter without stain!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can accomplish these four dharmas will attain the power of supernormal knowledges.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The body is as light as the mind; In all phenomena, there is no dependence.”
The space-element is immeasurable for me; I maintain the four elements with equanimity.
By contemplating these four dharmas, one attains immeasurable supernormal powers.
Through the power of this samādhi, one travels throughout all worlds.
In a single thought, they universally pervade everywhere and behold many thousands of billions of Buddhas.
"Daughter Without Stain!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas are exceptionally handsome and distinguished."
What are the four? First, being free from anger.
Second, sweeping the stūpas of the Tathāgata and shielding them from evil winds and rain, and feeling joy after having done so.
Third, they fully perfect the purity of their precepts and maintain them with protection.

Fourth, at all times, they are the first to inquire after others with kindness; seeing those who are vessels of the Dharma, they do not wish to harm them, and their minds are as adamantine as a vajra.
“Vimalā! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will be exceptionally handsome and distinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
Free from the stain of anger toward others, protecting the Buddha’s stūpas from wind and rain,
cleaning and adorning them with purity, always honoring and making offerings,
constantly upholding the pure precepts, and always being the first to inquire after others with a kind mind—
"Exerting oneself fully toward the vessel of the Dharma, like a vajra or Mount Sumeru.
Girl Without Stain!
Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish four dharmas, they are born by transformation and always remain in the presence of the Buddhas."
What are the four? First, to fashion an image of the Tathāgata in the lotus posture.
Second, to fill one’s cupped hands with *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, and either scatter them upon the body of the Buddha or scatter them over a stūpa.
Third, being at ease and possessing great faith and talent, one’s mind does not destroy any roots of goodness in those who uphold the precepts.
Fourth, one vows to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, causing them to attain the Buddha-way.
Daughter Vimalā! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will therefore be born by transformation and always remain in the presence of the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Forming the posture of the supreme lotus seat, In the likeness of the Tathāgata’s form, One offers handfuls full of water-lilies; This is for the benefit of others."
Not speaking ill of others, not grasping at the faults of others,
mindful of sentient beings in the ten directions, and wishing for them to have peace and happiness—
by practicing such fourfold supreme virtues, [one attains the fruit of the path].
Therefore, they attain birth by transformation and always remain in the presence of the Buddha. "Stainless Girl!
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas obtain great wealth and happiness."
What are the four?
First, giving with an impartial mind.
Second, giving without expecting a reward.
Third, her mind is opened and she possesses great faith.
Fourth, she is able to know the mental activities of sentient beings.
Daughter Without Stain!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can accomplish these four dharmas will attain great wealth and happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Giving with an impartial mind, Not begrudging anything one possesses,”
Deeply believing in the Buddha’s wisdom, one repeatedly attains great wealth and happiness.
Possessing faith and free from flattery or deception, one does not seize what belongs to others;
with faith in the Dharma and upright views, one attains excellent wealth and happiness.
“Daranirmala! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish four dharmas and thereby attain great wisdom. What are these four?
First, one does not give rise to envy toward the Dharma.
Second, one is able to remove the doubts and regrets of others.
Third, one speaks in accordance with what has been heard.
Fourth, they extensively cultivate the practice of emptiness.
Daughter Without Stain!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain great wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The wise person harbors no envy; They can dispel the doubts and regrets of others.
Speaking exactly as they have heard, They proclaim the Tathāgata’s practice of emptiness."
"By practicing these four dharmas, which the Tathāgata rejoices in,
and by training according to the Buddha's teaching, one attains the state of a Buddha,
the Honored One among bipeds. Daughter Without Stain!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish four dharmas and thereby attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*). What are these four?
First, they are able to preach the Dharma that ought to be heard to those who have long since forgotten it, causing them to remember and not forget the words and their meanings.
Second, to cause others to believe and desire [the Dharma] through speech, to gladden them, and to preach the Dharma for their sake;
third, to desire to lead them out of the various sufferings of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and into *nirvāṇa*.
Fourth, knowing the samādhi of illusion in accordance with one’s vows.
Daughter without Stain!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain the knowledge of past lives.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"For those who have long recited [the teachings] but now forget them, Instruct them so that they may remember;
Always speak words that are pleasant to hear, And teach others without weariness."
Causing them to emerge from the suffering of conditioned existence, They abandon signs and cultivate samādhi.
Practicing these four dharmas, One attains the status of a Great Man with knowledge of past lives;
Throughout immeasurable billions of thousands of kalpas, One swiftly becomes the foremost physician.
“Daranirmala! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have accomplished four dharmas always draw near to the Buddhas.
What are these four?
First, one shall not abandon the Buddha-dharma even for the sake of losing one's life.
Second, one shall never, even for the sake of losing one's life, speak of the faults or transgressions of the Dharma teacher.
Third, even at the cost of one's life, one shall never associate with unwholesome friends.
Fourth, one shall constantly cultivate the Buddha-recollection samādhi.
Daughter Without Stain!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can accomplish these four dharmas will always remain in close proximity to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Never abandoning the Buddha-way, Not disparaging the Dharma-preacher,”
Do not associate with evil friends, but always diligently keep the Buddha in mind.
By practicing these four dharmas, one shall draw near to the Tathāgata;
in whatever place one is born, there the Buddha will always be present.
"Until you have realized the path of unsurpassed bodhi,
in every place where you are born, may you always draw near to the Buddhas.
Daughter Without Stain!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain the thirty-two marks of a great man. What are these four?
First, they scatter gold over the Buddha, or scatter it over a stūpa.
Second, constantly anointing the stūpas of the Tathāgata with fragrant oil.
Third, making offerings of various flowers, incense, and music.
Fourth, accompanied by one’s retinue, making offerings to the upādhyāya, ācārya, and others.
Daughter Vimalā! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain the thirty-two marks of a great man.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Scattering gold upon a stūpa, Anointing the Buddha’s tower with fragrant oil,
Offering incense, flowers, and music— One makes offerings to the Teacher with a reverent heart."
By practicing these four dharmas, one attains the thirty-two marks, which are upright and most wondrous, endowed with all merits.
These dharmas possess sublime characteristics; such is the Buddha’s supreme wisdom.
“Daughter Vimalā, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain the eighty minor marks. What are these four?
First, adorning the Dharma-seat with various kinds of exquisite robes.”
Second, one does not give rise to weariness in making offerings to others.
Third, one does not engage in strife or discord with those who are Dharma masters.
Fourth, one teaches all sentient beings the practices for attaining the Bodhi of the Buddha.
“Daughter Without Stain!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain the eighty minor marks.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Adorning the Dharma-seat with exquisite robes, tirelessly making offerings to others,
and teaching sentient beings toward Bodhi— by practicing these four kinds of merit, a Bodhisattva easily attains the eighty minor marks.”
"At all times, they are adorned with supreme marks.
Daughter Without Stain!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain pure eloquence."
What are the four? First, upholding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Second, reading and reciting the Dharma-gates of the three aggregates day and night.
Third, to explain to others the Dharma of being apart from causes and conditions, because the Buddha’s bodhi is neither born nor extinguished and is apart from causes and conditions.
Fourth, to joyfully receive and uphold [the teaching], not begrudging one's body, life, or wealth.
“Daughter Vimalā! If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain pure eloquence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Day and night constantly reciting and chanting, firmly upholding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
though it may conflict with all worldly ways, one should receive and uphold this Buddha-dharma,
not begrudging body, life, or wealth, but cherishing that path to Bodhi."
By practicing these four dharmas, one attains an increase in eloquence;
like wearing various garlands, those who see them are filled with joy.
Among all the worlds, including humans, devas, and other sentient beings—
Seeing those bodhisattvas, one’s joy is likewise so.
"Daughter Vimalā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain a pure buddha-field."
What are the four? First, not being envious of others.
Second, maintaining an equal mind toward oneself and others.
Third, seeing all sentient beings, their minds are always joyful.
Fourth, they do not associate with evil companions.
Daughter Without Stain!
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who can accomplish these four dharmas will attain a pure buddha-field.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The mind harbors no jealousy, And does not covet the gains of others.”
Seeing sentient beings with joy, maintaining an impartial mind toward all,
and not associating with evil companions—
those who fully practice these four dharmas will attain a pure buddha-field.
“Daughter Vimalā! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who accomplish four dharmas attain the perfection of the Saṃgha. What are these four?
First, not to harbor thoughts regarding the retinues of others;
second, to reconcile those whose retinues have been divided;
third, to receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings] at places where the Dharma is expounded, and to explain them for the sake of others.
Fourth, they abandon harsh speech.
Daughter Without Stain!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Not dwelling on the retinues of others, One who reconciles those who are divided,
Teaching people in the place where the Dharma is preached, And refraining from speech that causes division."
By practicing these four dharmas, one attains the foremost pure Saṃgha.
Those who wish to attain the pure Saṃgha, O wise woman, should cultivate this dharma. “O stainless woman!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accomplish four dharmas by which they are born into Buddha-lands according to their heart's wishes.
What are these four?
First, they do not give rise to envy toward the friends and relatives of others.
Second, they constantly seek the six *pāramitās* with the desire to bring them to fulfillment.
Third, their mental faith is pure and firm.

Fourth, they always regard all bodhisattvas as their teachers; even toward those who have only recently resolved to attain awakening, they conceive the thought of them as teachers, making offerings to them without partial attachment to the influence of close friends.
Daughter Without Stain!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can accomplish these four dharmas, they will be born in buddha-fields according to their vows.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Do not envy the gains and offerings of others; Seek the excellence of the pāramitās;
Always maintain a pure and firm mind, Regarding the Bodhisattva as a teacher."
Without flattery, seeking the conditions for happiness, one desires that one's kin may obtain joy.
Constantly cultivating these merits, one will swiftly draw near to the Tathāgata;
according to the heart’s aspiration, one shall be born in the Buddha-world.
"Once born in that world, one shall obtain everything according to one's recollection.
At that time, the girl Vimalā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If I do not believe in, accept, cultivate, or practice this Dharma-door that the Buddha has taught for my sake, I would thereby destroy all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who currently live, exist, and remain present throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke thus to Vimalā:
"How extraordinary you are!

If it is as you say—that awakening is difficult to attain and the practice for that awakening is difficult to cultivate—then for a woman to be able to cultivate such practice is truly most extraordinary."
The girl Vimalā then made this vow:
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
In a future age, I shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, exactly equal to the present World-Honored One, without any difference."
If this is true and not false, let this trichiliocosm tremble in six ways, and let not a single sentient being feel fear.

By my truthful word, if I am indeed capable of practicing fully as the Buddha has taught, may flowers rain down now, may the celestial musicians spontaneously produce their sounds, and may my female body be transformed into that of a man.
When the girl Vimaladattā had spoken thus, at that very moment the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; celestial musical instruments spontaneously sounded, and a rain of various heavenly flowers fell.
The girl Vimalā transformed her female body into that of a man, appearing like a handsome youth of sixteen years; everyone beheld him.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
“How rare it is, World-Honored One!”

According to my understanding, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, this attainment of stainless supernormal powers is the most supreme; such great power, such a great essence, and such true maintenance—these and other such things are fully endowed with various distinct causes and conditions as they are perceived.
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha said: "So it is, so it is,
Maudgalyāyana!"

As you have said, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until reaching the site of awakening, that bodhisattva is a field of merit for the world’s devas and humans, surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, the Buddha smiled—a constant dharma of all Buddhas. When they smile, immeasurable and manifold colors, various distinct hues—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, crystal, and the color of gold and jewels—issue forth as light from their mouths. This light universally illumines immeasurable and countless worlds, reaching even up to the Brahma-world; having shone, it returns and enters the crown of the Tathāgata’s head. Then, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over his left shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse, asking:
“The King of the Kinnaras, Lord of the Sahā World, With the voice of Great Brahmā, And the melodic song of the Jīvajīvaka.”
The sounds of the devas of music bring tranquility to greed, hatred, and delusion;
the entire world conceives love for this stainless King of Men, the Moon,
whose power and merit are like the ocean.
For what reason do you emit this radiance and cause the earth to quake in six ways?
The great earth does not collapse, and celestial flowers rain down from the sky; those who behold them find their hearts filled with joy.
Just as the lion king destroys the small jackals,
so the Tathāgata can crush all those of external paths.
I pray only that the Honored Muni will explain this for me today.
The Buddha reflected: "By what causes and conditions, and who shall obtain this great benefit?
[There are those numbering] in the hundreds of millions and nayutas; the radiance of the sun, moon, and mani-jewels;
Śakra, lord of the Sahā world, and even the light of the Brahmā heavens."
From the Blessed One’s face, stainless and pure light radiates;
all the lights of the ten directions are thereby eclipsed.
His forehead is full like the moon, and the space between his brows is pure and free from defilement.
His brilliance is like the autumn moon and sun, no different from the *pundarīka* flower;
it is like the flashing of lightning, by which the glow of fireflies cannot appear.
The Honored One Śākyamuni outshines all non-Buddhist teachers.
"The Tathāgata now emits this light; who will receive its benefit?
After the Venerable Ānanda had spoken thus, the Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Do you see this Vimalaprabhā, who dwells in suchness, who has transformed her female body and attained the form of a man? Ānanda replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda! This Bodhisattva Vimalaprāpta practiced the bodhisattva conduct for eighty thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he practiced the bodhisattva conduct in the presence of sixty thousand asaṃkhyeya Buddhas before the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta finally gave rise to the mind of enlightenment.
The merit and adornment of the buddha-worlds of eighty thousand bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī is equal to the merit and adornment of a single buddha-world of the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhāsa.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā:
"Noble son! If you have been practicing the conduct of awakening and seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for such a long time, why has this female body not been transformed?"
Vimalā said: "Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
Awakening is neither a female body nor a male body."
"Why is this? Awakening is unarisen; it is not something awakened to by body or mind.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī spoke these words:
"Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaprabha is truly able to understand this profound liberation.
The Buddha said:

“Mañjuśrī! Just as the Bodhisattva Vimalaprāpta practiced the Brahma-conduct under sixty billion Buddhas, cultivated the samādhi of emptiness for eighty thousand asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and developed the patience of non-arising; and having posed difficult questions to thirty billion Buddhas, he was declared by those Buddhas to have attained a profound liberation that is foremost among all bodhisattvas; and having made offerings of clothing and food to eighty billion Buddhas, he inquired about this Dharma-gate of eloquence regarding the meaning of these treatises.”
Mañjuśrī! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears this Dharma-gate,
receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it extensively for others, that person will thereby obtain exceedingly great merit.
"Why is this? Because this Dharma-gate provides the complete causes and conditions for entering into Bodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what name should this Dharma-gate be called? How should I uphold it?”
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!
This Dharma gate is named ‘Eloquence in Discourse’; you should uphold it thus.”
"It is named 'The Dharma-Door of Attaining the Stainless'; thus should it be upheld.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, there were eighty billion nayutas of sentient beings, including devas and humans, all of whom attained non-retrogression and were destined to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Saṃghabhadra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! World-Honored One!”
“Vimalaprabhā Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, after how much time shall he attain the awakening of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaprapta, after passing through incalculable hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vimalahasitasmṛtidhvajarāja. His world shall be named Anantaviśuddhaguṇavyūha; in that land there will be no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and its prosperity and bliss will surpass those of the heavens.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalaprāpta, having heard his prophecy from the World-Honored One, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He ascended into the air to a height of eight billion tāla trees and remained suspended in mid-air, emitting a great radiance. This light shone throughout a thousand Buddha-worlds, and he came to rest upon a jeweled flower eighty-four thousand yojanas above the crown of the World-Honored One’s head. To make an offering to the Buddha, he descended like a bird, circumambulated the Buddha a thousand times, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and sat to one side.

At that time, those five hundred brahmins, together with the brahmin Brahmādeva, beholding the supreme supernatural powers of the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha, their body hair stood on end; they attained pure faith and gave rise to profound love and reverence.
Joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
“If one reveres the Tathāgata, that benefit is the greatest benefit;
for it causes a person to become certain, establishing the causal conditions for the Buddha-dharma.”
I am of the Brahmin caste; previously I committed evil deeds and, upon seeing a Great Śrāvaka teacher, spoke unwholesome words with my mouth.
Now I repent for this transgression, and pray that I shall not suffer its calamity hereafter.
Seeing the evil speech of the Buddha’s son, I realized it was not the talk of a worthy man;
he had not attained this human body well, but had wasted in vain the food and drink provided by others.
Had I not seen the Buddha, the King of Supreme and Wondrous Virtue, [I would have remained in ignorance].
Then, together with Vimalaprabhā, they departed, playing their instruments in harmony.
Upon seeing that son of the Buddha, I paid him respect for a brief moment and asked him:
"Where and when did you see the Buddha?
He replied: "Seven days after my birth, at that time I heard the name of the Buddha."
He spoke of the Buddha’s virtues, whose true substance is no different from what has been heard.
Having heard that Buddha’s name, I gave rise to deep and pure faith;
desiring to go to all [the lands], I turn toward unsurpassed bodhi.
By virtue of my previous roots of merit, I have been able to hear the name of the Buddha;
I have come before the Lion of the Śākyas and prostrated with my head at the Buddha’s feet.
Seeking to see the Buddha and pay him homage, I shall hear the unsurpassed Dharma.
Having seen this Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, one attains liberation from all suffering.
If the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the speaker of truthful words, preaches the Dharma,
may I study that Buddha-Dharma and obtain the causal conditions for the Buddha-Dharma.
Because this woman heard the Buddha’s Dharma, she attained unsurpassed bodhi;
I now enter the true Dharma, the gateway through which Bodhisattvas practice the Path.
Having faith and entering the Buddha’s Dharma, I shall surely attain supremacy in the world.
With a firm and resolute mind, he knows; He recollects the Honored Muni.
The Noble One, knowing through wisdom, was questioned by Ānanda, And bestowed a prediction upon all people.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"These five hundred individuals, brahmins and Brahmās,
shall all at one and the same time attain the path of Buddhahood.
For eighty billion kalpas, they shall commit no evil deeds."
In each and every eon, he beheld a hundred million Tathāgatas.
Having already made offerings to them in the past, he fulfilled his service to five hundred Buddhas;
thereafter, he again beheld a hundred million Buddhas seated at the seat of enlightenment.
Making offerings to the Sangha, the field of merit, To eighty billion bhikṣus,
he extensively expounded Such a Dharma gate for the sake of all sentient beings.
In succession, they all attained The bliss of tranquil nirvana.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas Vādipūjita and Vimalaprabha, along with all the other bodhisattvas, those śrāvakas, those brahmins, King Prasenajit, Lord of Kośala, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Girl Vimalā Obtaining Immaculateness
